title: Building Reliable Classes
lede: Turn Week 5's class syntax into working models: define valid state, preserve it through methods, trace references, separate shared data from instance data, and connect objects through composition.

sections.title: Contracts and valid state
concepts:
A class is useful when it gives the rest of the program a dependable promise. A stock item starts with a non-negative quantity; a successful withdrawal reduces it by exactly the requested positive amount; a rejected withdrawal changes nothing. These rules are its invariant and method contract.

Write down the inputs, result and state change before writing the method body. Test zero, negative amounts, exactly the available quantity and one too many. A getter reports a value; a mutator changes the model. Keeping these jobs clear makes a failing test easier to explain.
Hide the path around the rule

Java private prevents an outside caller from assigning a field directly. Python _stock communicates intended use but does not enforce privacy. In either language, public methods should be the normal route for changing state. Constructor validation must establish the same invariant that later methods preserve; these small examples assume a valid starting quantity.

sections.title: References and object lifetime
concepts: b = a copies a reference in both languages. Draw two arrows to one object, then trace a mutating call through either arrow. Creating another object requires another constructor call. Two objects with equal field values need not be the same object.
Instance collections belong in the constructor

A Python list in the class body is shared. A list assigned to self.items in __init__ is created for each instance. Compare that rule with Java instance fields and static fields. Before explaining output, count allocations, not variable names.

sections.title: Shared data and instance data
concepts: A counter is a deliberate shared responsibility

A shared ticket counter is appropriate when every new ticket must receive the next number. The ticket's own number is instance data. Updating the shared counter later does not rewrite existing ticket numbers.

Appending to a shared class list changes that one list. Assigning a.items = [] instead creates an instance attribute that shadows the class attribute for a. This is why the location of allocation matters more than whether the expression contains an object name.

notes: static int count

final int number
Assign an individual number once for this ticket.
examples.why: The shared counter reaches 2; a keeps its previously assigned number 1.

examples.title: A class attribute can share too much
examples.code:
class Basket:
    items = []

a = Basket()
b = Basket()
a.items.append("tea")
print(b.items)
print(a.items is b.items)
notes: items = []
This list is constructed in the class body and shared by these instances.
a.items.append

wrong:
[]
False

examples.why: Both objects find the class attribute. Move the list into __init__ to give each basket its own storage.

sections.title: Composition and a small public interface
concepts: A shelf holds a book; it is not a special kind of book. A field that refers to another object expresses this composition. Give the class with the data the job that uses it: Book knows its title, while Shelf decides how to describe its contents.

A useful string representation helps a person inspect state while debugging. Return a string from __str__; do not print inside it. In Java the corresponding method is toString(). Keep presentation separate from the operations that update the model, so a formatting change does not change the rules.

questions.q: Which input best tests the lower boundary of take(amount)?
questions.correct: Zero, because the contract requires a positive amount.
wrong: A very large positive number, because it tests only the upper limit of available stock.
Any positive number smaller than the stock, because ordinary success proves all boundaries.
A second object with the same quantity, because identity always determines numeric validity.
questions.why: Zero tests the positive-amount condition; negative values are also useful. A valid ordinary amount does not test rejection.

questions.q: What does Java private contribute to the stock model?
questions.correct: It prevents outside code from directly assigning the field.
wrong: It automatically rejects every negative value passed to any method of the class.
It guarantees that every method in the class preserves the correct stock invariant.
It makes all stock objects share one common copy of the private field.
questions.why: The compiler restricts field access. The constructor and methods must still implement the validation.

questions.q: Which relationship is best represented by composition?
wrong: A triangle is a polygon, so it must contain a polygon instead of being one.
Every Java object is a String because print can display its representation.
Two variables refer to one object, so one variable inherits from the other.
questions.why: A has-a relationship is represented by a member referring to a collaborator.

questions.q: How should you check a state-changing method?
questions.correct: Check its return value and the resulting observable state.
wrong: Check only that it printed a success message, ignoring changes to the object state.
Check only that it compiled, because the type checker proves every business rule.
Check only one successful call, since a rejection cannot possibly change any data.
questions.why: A method can return the expected flag while corrupting its state. Rejected operations also need state checks.

exercises.title: An inventory that refuses invalid requests
exercises.brief: Read an initial stock, a request count, then that many amounts. Print OK or Refused per request, then the remaining stock. Accept only positive amounts no larger than the current stock. The initial stock is non-negative.

exercises.title: Inventory in Python
exercises.brief: Implement the same stock contract as exercise 1. Input: initial stock, request count, then one amount per line. Print OK or Refused for each request, then the stock. Store the stock on an Inventory instance.
exercises.starter:
class Inventory:
    # __init__, take and available
    pass

stock = int(input())
n = int(input())
# process n requests
exercises.solution:
class Inventory:
    def __init__(self, stock): self._stock = stock
    def take(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0 or amount > self._stock: return False
        self._stock -= amount
        return True
    def available(self): return self._stock

item = Inventory(int(input()))
n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    print("OK" if item.take(int(input())) else "Refused")
print(item.available())

exercises.title: A readable book
exercises.brief: Read a title, then a non-negative page count. Implement Book.__str__ so printing the object produces exactly Title (N pages). The title may contain spaces.
exercises.starter:
class Book:
    # __init__ and __str__
    pass

title=input()
pages=int(input())
# construct and print the book
exercises.solution:
class Book:
    def __init__(self,title,pages): self.title,self.pages=title,pages
    def __str__(self): return f"{self.title} ({self.pages} pages)"

print(Book(input(),int(input())))

activities: Write a contract for borrow() and returnBook(). Identify the fields, valid states and rejected requests. One person proposes edge cases, another draws object references, and a third explains how the methods preserve the rules.
